No. Cleanup restores service, but leaves the demonstrated race intact: both writers can see “absent” before either inserts.

Enforce atomic uniqueness on command ID in the store, covering both writers. Treat the insert outcome as authoritative. On a uniqueness conflict, retrieve the existing command, confirm the payload matches, and return its existing result. A different payload must follow the contract’s conflict handling; it must not silently receive the existing result.

Use cleanup only to remove existing duplicates before enabling the constraint. Coordinate that transition so concurrent writes cannot introduce duplicates between cleanup and activation. Rerun the supplied concurrent reproduction against the fix.

This is the smallest structural change supported by the evidence. It adds duplicate-conflict handling but requires no new coordination service. It establishes storage uniqueness; it does not by itself prove payment side effects execute only once.

## Architectural Invariants

| Invariant | Scope | Verification | Enforcement | Failure impact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Each accepted command ID has at most one stored command. | Shared command store, across both writers and retries. | **Violated** in the supplied reproduction. After the fix, rerun it and check existing records. | **Proposed:** store-level atomic uniqueness on command ID; capability supplied, activation unverified. | Duplicate accepted commands and recurring cleanup. |
| A duplicate retry returns the existing result only when its payload matches the stored command. | Duplicate handling in both writers. | **Unverified:** test matching and differing payloads against an existing ID. | **Proposed:** payload comparison in each writer’s uniqueness-conflict path. | A different command could be incorrectly acknowledged as the original. |
